name: Macmillan Cancer Support: information, support and care for people with cancer in the UK (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: Macmillan works only in the UK.
summary: Macmillan Cancer Support helps people with cancer in the UK: a phone line with cancer nurses, information advisers and welfare rights advisers, an online community, information centres, volunteer Buddies and small grants, plus learning for the 11,100 NHS nurses and other professionals in its network, funding for community and end-of-life care, and grants to community groups. Our model of all its charitable spending in 2025 (£112m in the year; 476,000 people with cancer supported) values the support by its effect on wellbeing, from trials of telephone and online support for people with cancer, and the welfare benefits its advisers help people claim on the site's log-income scale, net of what they cost taxpayers. It comes to about {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000, because the help is light (a call or two, or reading a forum) for people who already have NHS care, and its biggest money gain, benefits identified at about £8,500 a year for each of 13,200 households (about £5,100 awarded), is mostly a transfer from other UK households that are only somewhat richer. About half of the result comes from those benefits. Every branch but the grants (audited money paid) is discounted for missing data, since none of Macmillan's services has a controlled evaluation: the Support Line, Buddies and online support, welfare rights, the professionals and the posts its grants paid for, and the community and system work. The biggest uncertainties are how much of the identified benefits are paid and would not have been claimed anyway, and how far below average the claimants' consumption is; with every judgment at its ends the result spans over a thousandfold, so it is mostly uncertainty.

So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

rows.explainer: Macmillan's figure for the benefits these people could be eligible for; how many years of payments it stands for and the share awarded are rows below.

rows.label: Years of payments the £112m stands for
rows.explainer: Judgment: the report doesn't say; benefit-advice services usually report gains as a year's worth. Cross-check: Moffatt, Noble and White (2012) measured a Macmillan-funded welfare rights service in County Durham at a median gain of £70.30 a week (2009-10), about £3,660 a year, or about £5,600 in 2025 prices (UK CPI ×1.53 since 2010); the model at its defaults gives £5,090 a year per household awarded (£8,485 identified × 60%). 1 (0.7-1.5): the low end if the figure counts only the months left in the year of the claim (claims are made through the year, so a year's figure can hold less than a year's payments), the high end if it includes arrears or more than a year of payments.

source.title: Macmillan Cancer Support, Annual Report and Accounts 2025 (year to 31 December 2025, audited)

rows.label: Average grant to an individual
rows.explainer: The pilot's grant was a one-off £350 to over 500 people (p. 19: "we provided a one-off grant of £350 to over 500 people"); older Macmillan Grants were similar in size. 350 (250-600): the higher end if some grants were larger hardship payments.

rows.label: People given a grant
rows.explainer: Grants paid over the average grant.

rows.label: Macmillan professionals at the end of 2025

source.title: Macmillan Cancer Support, Annual Report and Accounts 2025 (year to 31 December 2025, audited)
source.quote: By the end of 2025, there were just over 11,100 Macmillan professionals

rows.explainer: Nurses, support workers, allied health professionals, GPs and psychological therapists in NHS and other posts who belong to Macmillan's professional community (besides 4,000 Boots Macmillan pharmacists, not counted).

rows.label: Share of the grants paid in 2025 that paid for NHS posts (Macmillan professionals' first years)
rows.explainer: Judgment. Until 2024 Macmillan's main grants were multi-year commitments to NHS bodies to fund new Macmillan posts for their first years (the report: "we are moving away from our historical approach of funding individual posts for a fixed, short-term period of time", p. 24); the £56.6m paid in 2025 is mostly on those commitments, the rest on information and support centres, Improving the Cancer Journey, community and research grants. Half (30%-70%).

rows.label: Cost of a funded post for a year
rows.explainer: Judgment: a band 6-7 NHS cancer nurse specialist or allied health professional, with employer's national insurance and pension (about 30% on pay of £38,000-£55,000), about £60,000 (£45,000-£80,000).

rows.label: Post-years paid for by the grants
rows.explainer: Grants paid for posts over a post-year's cost.

rows.label: People with cancer each professional supports in a year
rows.explainer: Judgment: a cancer clinical nurse specialist carries a caseload of a few hundred new patients a year, support workers and therapists fewer; Macmillan says the 11,100 support "hundreds of thousands of people living with cancer" (p. 24), i.e. 20-60 each counted once across professionals. 100 (40-300), counting a patient once per professional.

rows.label: System Transformation: spending per person who gets the funded local care
rows.explainer: Judgment. The area's expensed spending pays for grants and staff behind services such as Improving the Cancer Journey in Scotland (council link officers doing holistic needs assessments: in Glasgow six full-time officers saw 6,130 people over 2015-2020, roughly £250-£400 a person), end-of-life care services (dearer per person) and advocacy that reaches nobody directly; the Neighbourhood Transformation Funds' social investments (£23.2m committed) are loans held on the balance sheet, not in this spending. £1,000 (£300-£4,000).

rows.label: People given proactive community or end-of-life care by funded services
rows.explainer: The area's in-year spending (the year's activities) over the cost per person; grants paid on earlier commitments for this area are in the cost but not in this reach, a difference of under 1% of the result.

rows.label: Communities and Participation: spending per person reached
rows.explainer: Judgment: small grants to community groups and Cancer Champions who connect people from groups with worse experiences to support (talks, sessions, signposting). No reach published; £300 (£100-£1,000), between a light-touch community session and a case-worked referral.

rows.label: People reached by funded community groups and Cancer Champions
rows.explainer: The area's spending over the cost per person.

rows.explainer: 0 here: each branch below has its own effect, duration and adjustments, summed in the bridges.

rows.label: Years the effect lasts (canonical row)
rows.explainer: 1: unused, the branches have their own.

rows.label: WELLBYs per person (canonical row)
rows.explainer: Point-years, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Support Line call: wellbeing gain, in standard deviations

source.title: Zhang et al., Effectiveness of telephone-based interventions on health-related quality of life and prognostic outcomes in breast cancer patients and survivors: a meta-analysis (Eur J Cancer Care, 2018)
source.quote: SMD = -0.16, 95% CI [0.01, 0.30] for anxiety (14 studies, 2,002 participants), as reported in the abstract

rows.explainer: Telephone-delivered psychosocial support for people with cancer reduces anxiety by about 0.16 SD (meta-analysis of 14 trials, 2,002 women with breast cancer: "SMD = -0.16"), with depression effects in the same direction but not significant (the abstract prints the anxiety CI as [0.01, 0.30], its sign flipped against the point estimate) and quality of life SMD 0.54; those were structured multi-session programmes. A Support Line contact is usually one or two calls, so about half: 0.08 (0.02-0.2).

rows.label: Buddies (8-12 calls with a trained volunteer): wellbeing gain, in standard deviations
rows.explainer: A course of regular supportive calls is close to the multi-session telephone programmes of the meta-analysis above (0.16 SD on anxiety), delivered by trained volunteers rather than professionals: 0.12 (0.04-0.3).

rows.label: Online Community, website and print only: wellbeing gain, in standard deviations

source.title: McCaughan et al. (2017), Online support groups for women with breast cancer, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews CD011652
source.quote: Pooled data from two studies (120 women) showed a small to moderate reduction in depression (SMD -0.37, 95% CI -0.75 to 0.00; very low-quality evidence).

rows.explainer: The Cochrane review of online support groups for women with breast cancer found a small reduction in depression at the end of the intervention (SMD -0.37, 95% CI -0.75 to 0.00, two trials, very low-quality evidence) and no effect on quality of life (SMD -0.11). Those were structured groups; most of these people read the forum or the website's information a few times. 0.02 (0.005-0.08): a twentieth of the trials' point estimate, the high end a fifth.

rows.label: Years a Support Line or online gain lasts
rows.explainer: Judgment: the trials measured at the end of support or a few months later; a call's relief at a hard moment fades within months. 0.25 (0.1-0.5), the gain falling linearly to nothing.

rows.label: Years a Buddies gain lasts
rows.explainer: Judgment: the calls run for 2-3 months, and some of the gain lasts beyond them: 0.5 (0.25-1), falling linearly.

rows.label: WELLBYs per Support Line caller
rows.explainer: SDs × the site's WELLBYs per SD-year × half the duration (a linear fade), discounted.

rows.label: WELLBYs per person with a Buddy
rows.explainer: As above.

rows.label: WELLBYs per online or print user
rows.explainer: As above.

rows.label: Share of a professional's patients whose care is better because of Macmillan's learning and support
rows.explainer: Judgment. Posts in their first years paid by Macmillan's grants are credited in the posts branch; the rest are paid by the NHS (Macmillan moved away from funding posts). What this area's money buys is conferences, e-learning (1,700 attended virtual events), development grants and the eHNA care-planning platform. A small share of their patients get noticeably better personalised or psychological care because of it: 3% (0.5%-10%).

rows.label: Wellbeing gain for a patient whose care is better, in standard deviations
rows.explainer: Judgment anchored on the telephone psychosocial meta-analysis (0.16 SD on anxiety for a full programme): better holistic needs assessment, care planning and communication by the patient's own nurse is of that order: 0.1 (0.03-0.25).

rows.label: Years that gain lasts
rows.explainer: Judgment: through a course of treatment, 0.5 (0.25-1), falling linearly.

rows.label: WELLBYs per patient whose care is better
rows.explainer: As for the Support Line.

rows.label: Share of the funded posts that wouldn't have existed in those years without Macmillan
rows.explainer: Judgment: Macmillan pays a post's first years and the NHS takes it on; some posts would have been created anyway, a little later. 0.4 (0.2-0.7).

rows.label: Proactive community or end-of-life care: wellbeing gain per person, in standard deviations
rows.explainer: Judgment. Trials of proactive, assessment-led community care for frail older people (comprehensive geriatric assessment, case management) show small and inconsistent gains in quality of life and wellbeing, around 0.1 SD where positive; end-of-life care and link-worker support for people with cancer similar. 0.1 (0.02-0.25).

rows.label: Years that gain lasts
rows.explainer: Judgment: support that runs for a year or more while the person is enrolled: 1 (0.5-2), falling linearly.

rows.label: WELLBYs per person given the funded care
rows.explainer: As above.

rows.label: Community groups and Cancer Champions: wellbeing gain per person, in standard deviations
rows.explainer: Judgment: lighter than a Support Line call for most (a talk, a session, signposting), more for the few connected to support they would have missed: 0.05 (0.01-0.15).

rows.label: WELLBYs per person reached by community groups
rows.explainer: As above, over the Support Line's duration.

rows.label: Welfare benefits awarded per person in a claimant's household, per year
rows.formula: wr_identified_gbp / wr_years_in_figure * wr_award_share / wr_households * usd_per_gbp / household_size
rows.explainer: The identified benefits for a year × the share awarded, per claimant household, spread over the household.

rows.label: Share of the identified benefits actually awarded
rows.explainer: Judgment. In Macmillan's welfare rights service in County Durham, claims made were successful 96% of the time (Moffatt et al. 2012, PLoS ONE: "Welfare benefit claims were successful for 96% of claims made"), but Macmillan's figure here is benefits people "could be eligible for": not everyone claims, and some die before an award. 60% (35%-85%).

rows.label: UK household-survey consumption per person, 2025, in dollars
rows.explainer: The site's UK national-accounts consumption per person (2024, dollars) × the shared survey-to-national-accounts ratio, back to pounds at 2024's rate, to 2025 prices with UK CPI and to dollars at 2025's rate.

rows.label: Claimants' consumption per person as a share of the UK survey average
rows.explainer: Judgment anchored on UK data: the poorest fifth of households spent £407.30 a week in the year to March 2025 against £676.60 for all households (ONS Family spending in the UK, https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/personalandhouseholdfinances/expenditure/bulletins/familyspendingintheuk/april2024tomarch2025), 0.60 per household and higher per person since poorer households are smaller. People who call for benefits advice are mostly in the lower half (many are pensioners claiming Attendance Allowance or people out of work through illness; a diagnosis costs those affected over £1,000 a month, p. 19), but not all in the poorest fifth: 0.65 (0.45-0.9).

rows.label: Claimants' consumption per person per year
Years the benefits are paid
rows.explainer: Judgment: disability and carer's benefits run while the illness lasts; some claimants are terminally ill (fast-track claims) and some recover. 1.5 (0.75-3).

rows.label: Log-consumption gain per person from benefits
rows.explainer: The site's one log-income scale at the claimants' own consumption, over the years the benefits run, discounted.

rows.label: Grant per person in the household
rows.explainer: One-off, spent within the year.

rows.label: Log-consumption gain per person from a grant
rows.explainer: One year's consumption raised by the grant.

rows.label: Marginal cost of public funds: what a pound of public money costs those who pay
rows.explainer: The site's shared figure (facts/public_funds.json): 1.2, range 1 (money shifted from other spending) to 1.5.

rows.label: UK: how the taxes behind benefits fall, relative to a tax proportional to consumption
rows.explainer: On the log scale a pound taken from someone costs 1 over their consumption, so a tax proportional to consumption costs 1 over the survey mean the claimants are measured on (a multiple of 1); a progressive tax costs less (above 1). UK taxes as a whole take a similar share of gross income across income fifths (ONS, Effects of taxes and benefits on household income), so against consumption, which is more equal than income, they are mildly progressive. 1.1, range 0.85 (money taken from other spending on poorer people) to 1.5.

rows.label: Taxpayers' log-consumption loss per dollar of benefits paid
rows.explainer: Benefits are paid by taxpayers (or by spending cut elsewhere), spread thinly over many people: each dollar costs the marginal cost of public funds over the payers' consumption.

rows.label: Healthy years gained other than through wellbeing and income
rows.explainer: 0: no trial of information or support services for people with cancer shows changes in illness or survival; their measured effects are on anxiety, depression and quality of life, counted as wellbeing above.

rows.label: Deaths averted per person
rows.explainer: 0: support services aren't shown to change survival; suicides averted by emotional support are possible but unmeasured (in the unmodelled share).

rows.label: Deaths under 5 (unused)
rows.explainer: 0: no deaths are modelled.

rows.label: Deaths aged 5-14 (unused)
rows.explainer: 0: no deaths are modelled.

rows.label: Deaths aged 15-49 (unused)
rows.explainer: 0: no deaths are modelled.

rows.label: Value of a death averted (unused)
rows.explainer: GiveWell's moral weights by the age band of each death, times your value of a life: the site's one value of a death.

rows.label: Trust in the support effects (Support Line, Buddies, online, professionals, community)
rows.explainer: Judgment: the anchors are small trials of self-reported anxiety and depression, mostly in women with breast cancer, with publication bias likely; scaled down for lighter contact already. 0.7 (0.4-1).

rows.label: Share of the support people wouldn't have got elsewhere
rows.explainer: Judgment: the trials' effects are against care as usual, but without Macmillan many callers and readers would turn to their NHS nurse, Cancer Research UK's nurse helpline, Maggie's centres or other forums, at some cost in time and quality. 0.6 (0.35-0.85).

rows.label: Share of the benefits that wouldn't have been claimed without the welfare rights team
rows.explainer: Judgment: many people with cancer never claim what they are entitled to, and a specialist adviser finds entitlements they don't know of; but some would have claimed through Citizens Advice, a hospital's own Macmillan benefits adviser (counted here only once) or unaided. 0.5 (0.25-0.75).

rows.label: Share of grants people wouldn't have got elsewhere
rows.explainer: Judgment: other cancer and hardship charities give small grants, but few and slowly; 0.85 (0.6-1).

rows.label: Share of the funded community care that wouldn't have existed without Macmillan
rows.explainer: Judgment: the NHS commissions some proactive and end-of-life care itself, and the national plans now ask for it, so some of these services would have come later anyway: 0.5 (0.25-0.8).

rows.label: Macmillan's share of the resources behind the funded services
rows.explainer: Judgment: the services are run with NHS trusts and local partners who add staff and money (the West Hertfordshire service is a partnership with the hospital trust and Social Finance): 0.6 (0.35-0.9).

rows.label: Years from spending to the funded care reaching people
rows.explainer: Judgment: the 2025 commitments fund services that start over the following year and run 3-6 years: 1 (0.5-2).

source.title: Macmillan Cancer Support, Annual Report and Accounts 2025 (year to 31 December 2025, audited)
source.quote: Our brilliant community of more than 31,000 volunteers gave more than 103,000 hours of their time.

rows.explainer: Mostly fundraising and the Buddies service.

rows.label: Value of a volunteer hour
rows.explainer: The shared UK value of a volunteer hour (@united_kingdom.volunteer_hour_value_2025, £17.96: median hourly pay, ONS, April 2025).

rows.label: Macmillan's share of the resources behind its own services
rows.explainer: Its cost over its cost plus volunteers' time (Convention 2); almost 1.

rows.label: Attribution share
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Share of the reported reach that got the help as counted
rows.explainer: Judgment: the counts are Macmillan's own administrative counts (unique users of services, callers), not audited; some online users are counted on thin engagement. 0.9 (0.7-1).

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: 1: Macmillan is 99% funded by public donations and its services are not ones government would otherwise fund at the margin; the social investments' repayments are in the unmodelled share.

rows.label: Years a gift waits before it is spent
rows.explainer: Judgment: Macmillan ended 2025 with £134m of funds against £175m of spending, having saved much of an exceptional legacy year for its new strategy; a pound given now is spent within the year or the next: 0.5 (0.2-1).

rows.label: Discount for the wait before spending
rows.explainer: The gift's wait, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Missing-data discount (canonical, weighted over branches)
rows.explainer: Every branch is thin (no controlled evaluation of Macmillan's own services; reach partly judged), so each takes $missing_data_discount; this is their weighted mean.

rows.label: Missing-data discount: Support Line, Buddies and online
rows.explainer: Thin: Macmillan's counts of people supported meet effects from trials of other, more structured telephone and online programmes.

rows.label: Missing-data discount: welfare rights and grants
rows.explainer: Thin: the money identified is Macmillan's own count, but what was awarded and what would have been claimed anyway are not measured.

rows.label: Missing-data discount: professionals
rows.explainer: Thin: no measure of how Macmillan's learning offer changes patients' care.

rows.label: Missing-data discount: posts paid for by grants
rows.explainer: Thin: the share of grants that paid for posts, the posts' caseloads and their patients' gain are judged; no measure of what the posts did.

rows.label: Missing-data discount: system transformation and communities
rows.explainer: Thin: no reach or outcomes published yet for the funded services.

rows.label: Adjustments: Support Line, Buddies and online
rows.formula: support_evidence_adj * support_counterfactual_adj * attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount * support_missing_data_adj

rows.label: Adjustments: welfare rights
rows.formula: wr_counterfactual_adj * attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount * wr_missing_data_adj

rows.label: Missing-data discount: grants
rows.explainer: 1, measured: the grants paid are audited (note 11) and valued by the site's log-consumption rule; only the counterfactual is judged, which has its own row.

rows.label: Counterfactual adjustment (weighted over branches)
rows.formula: (support_dalys_unadjusted * support_counterfactual_adj + wr_dalys_unadjusted * wr_counterfactual_adj + grant_dalys_unadjusted * grant_counterfactual_adj + system_dalys_unadjusted * system_counterfactual_adj + communities_dalys_unadjusted * support_counterfactual_adj + prof_dalys_unadjusted * prof_counterfactual_adj + posts_dalys_unadjusted * posts_counterfactual_adj) / (support_dalys_unadjusted + wr_dalys_unadjusted + grant_dalys_unadjusted + system_dalys_unadjusted + communities_dalys_unadjusted + prof_dalys_unadjusted + posts_dalys_unadjusted)
rows.explainer: The branches' counterfactual shares weighted by their unadjusted outcomes.

rows.label: Total adjustment (weighted over branches)
rows.formula: (support_dalys + wr_dalys + grant_dalys + prof_dalys + posts_dalys + system_dalys + communities_dalys) / (support_dalys_unadjusted + wr_dalys_unadjusted + grant_dalys_unadjusted + prof_dalys_unadjusted + posts_dalys_unadjusted + system_dalys_unadjusted + communities_dalys_unadjusted)
rows.explainer: Adjusted over unadjusted outcomes, all branches.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of the gross value (before the taxpayers' cost)
rows.explainer: Not modelled: carers and families helped by the Support Line and Online Community (+; about a third of callers are family), suicides averted by emotional support (+, small), the energy advice team's savings (+), information that helps people present earlier or follow treatment (+), advocacy on national cancer plans (+), social investments repaid and recycled into new services (+), hospital admissions the funded services avert (+, money the NHS spends elsewhere); against them, funging of NHS posts and services Macmillan's presence lets commissioners skip (-). As a share of the gross value (the claimants' benefits before the taxpayers' cost, so its sign doesn't flip with the net), about +5% (-3% to +15%).
